result.rationale: The diff shows `const message = `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`;` followed by `showToast(message || t("unable_to_add_guests"), ...)`. A template literal is always non-empty/truthy, so the fallback is unreachable dead code, and when `err.data?.code` is undefined the toast literally displays 'undefined: ...'. Additionally `t(err.message)` passes a raw error key like 'booking_not_found' (which the handler throws) to translation. This is a genuine, verifiable UX defect in newly added code.

judged_text: The onError toast builds `"${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}"`, a template literal that is always truthy, so the `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` fallback can never render and err.data?.code renders as the literal string 'undefined' when code is absent. Users see toasts like 'undefined: booking_not_found' — the server's raw translation key shown untranslated alongside 'undefined', misdirecting the user; the intended human-readable fallback is dead code.

adjudication.rationale: In `AddGuestsDialog.tsx` the onError handler builds `const message = `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`;` and then calls `showToast(message || t("unable_to_add_guests"), "error")`. A template literal always yields a truthy string (even when `err.data?.code` is `undefined`), so the `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` fallback is effectively dead code. This can also surface as user-facing toasts like `"undefined: ..."` when `err.data?.code` is absent.
